label: Rosa (designated caretaker)
tagline: Six years holding a family together: two kids growing up, two parents growing older, one estate slowly getting its paperwork done.

entries.title: Mateo starts kindergarten
entries.body: Mateo Ruiz, 5, walked into Lincoln Elementary holding my hand and let go at the door. Lucia Ruiz, 2, waved like a mayor. I cried in the car, then bought celebratory churros.

entries.title: Mom's diagnosis
entries.body: Carmen Vega diagnosed with early heart failure. Manageable, the cardiologist said, with medication and salt discipline. I am now the family medical secretary, apparently. Starting a list.

entries.title: Carmen Vega — Mom
entries.body: Carmen Vega, 71. Retired seamstress, unbeatable cook, allergic to being helped. Strategy: never say 'let me do that for you' — say 'teach me how you do it'. Works every time.

entries.title: Parents' wills — first draft
entries.body: Estate attorney drafted wills for Carmen and Jose Vega. Signing scheduled, then postponed, then forgotten. This folder is my nemesis. Future me: finish this.

entries.title: Jose Vega — Dad
entries.body: Jose Vega, 74. Retired bus driver, fixes anything with a motor and most things without. Starting to forget small things. Watching quietly for now.

entries.title: Two-household budget
entries.body: We quietly cover Mom's prescriptions and Dad's car insurance now. Built a shared spreadsheet with Andres Ruiz so the help is sustainable, not heroic. $420/month, planned and calm.

entries.title: Mom's medication list v2
entries.body: Carmen's list after the cardiology change: morning diuretic, evening statin, pill box filled Sundays by me. Printed copy on her fridge, photo on my phone.

entries.title: Lucia starts preschool
entries.body: Lucia Ruiz, 4, marched in with Mateo's old backpack. Both kids in school four mornings a week. I sat in a silent house and didn't know what to do with my hands.

entries.title: Estate paperwork: finish line
entries.body: Goal before year-end: wills signed, powers of attorney done, one folder with everything. The attorney has the drafts. I need two signatures and one notary. That's all. Do it.

entries.title: Powers of attorney — signed
entries.body: Done, finally: healthcare and financial POA for both parents, notarized, copies with the attorney and in the blue folder. The wills remain unsigned. One dragon left.

entries.title: POA before you need it
entries.body: Powers of attorney took three years of dread and one afternoon of signing — because we started before any crisis. The lesson I tell everyone: paperwork is easiest exactly when it feels least urgent.

entries.title: Dad's memory check
entries.body: Primary care ran Jose's memory screening: mild changes, recheck in a year. Driving still fine. We agreed: I ride along monthly, no drama, just data.

entries.title: Parent-teacher night, both schools
entries.body: Mateo (3rd grade) reads above level, forgets homework exists. Lucia (kindergarten) runs the classroom's feelings corner. Two schools, one evening, very tired feet.

entries.title: Care fund, formalized
entries.body: Opened a separate savings account for parent care: $300/month auto-transfer. When the house needs a ramp or Mom needs a device, the money conversation is already over.

entries.title: Wills — signed at last
entries.body: Three years after the first draft: Carmen and Jose signed their wills. Beneficiaries checked, executor is me, copies distributed. The nemesis folder is complete. I could frame it.

entries.title: Mom's medication list v3
entries.body: Cardiologist adjusted Carmen's dosage after the summer swelling. List updated everywhere: fridge, phone, blue folder. Version numbers on care documents forever now.

entries.title: Four generations, one table
entries.body: Christmas: kids performed a play, Dad fixed the oven mid-roast, Mom directed seating like a general. This is the whole point of the paperwork years. Wrote it down so I remember.

entries.title: Respite plan
entries.body: Andres and I agreed: one weekend a quarter, my sister covers parents, we disappear. Caretaking is a marathon; scheduled rest is part of the care, not a reward for it.

entries.title: The blue folder system
entries.body: One folder per person: current medication list (versioned), signed legal docs, insurance cards, one page of who-to-call. Updated every time anything changes, reviewed every November. Boring, portable, priceless.

entries.title: Dad stops driving at night
entries.body: Family agreement after the recheck: Jose keeps daytime driving, I handle nights and freeways. Framed as headlights, not capability. He grumbled, then agreed. Dignity preserved, risk down.

entries.title: Estate review due
entries.body: Annual review of the blue folder: wills current, POAs current, care fund healthy. This review used to take three years of dread. Now it takes one afternoon. Systems beat willpower.

entries.title: Mateo, double digits soon
entries.body: Mateo turns 10 next month and Lucia is reading chapter books to ME now. The kids are growing up on schedule. The parents are growing older on schedule. My job is to keep both schedules gentle.
